what: Xometry runs a marketplace for custom-manufactured parts. An engineer uploads a drawing, the system quotes a price and lead time automatically, and the job is routed to one of thousands of machine shops with spare capacity. It also sells industrial supplies through Thomas, the sourcing platform it acquired.
customers: Engineers and procurement staff at manufacturers, aerospace and medical device firms and research organisations who need small quantities of machined, printed or moulded parts. On the other side, small machine shops seeking work to fill idle machines.
money: Custom parts manufacturing: CNC machining, 3D printing, sheet metal and injection moulding, fulfilled by partner shops.
Advertising and sourcing services sold to suppliers through the Thomas platform.
moat: The instant quoting engine is the real asset: pricing a custom machined part normally takes a human estimator days, and Xometry's algorithm does it in seconds using data from millions of past quotes. Each additional job improves the pricing model, and the two-sided network gets more useful as both buyers and shops join.
risks: The company is still loss-making: about $17.3M of net loss and roughly negative $19.4M of free cash flow in the trailing period, though both are now close to breakeven.
The shares trade at about 7.3 times sales for a marketplace with thin gross margins, because the cost of the manufactured part is a cost of revenue.
Margins are structurally limited: Xometry must quote a price attractive to the buyer and still pay the machine shop, so the take rate has a ceiling.
Large customers can negotiate better terms or go direct to shops once they know who made their parts.
Debt of $347.7M against $219.1M of cash is notable for a company not yet profitable.
opportunities: Revenue has grown strongly every year, from $218.3M in 2021 to $686.6M in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $879.3M.
Losses have narrowed substantially, so profitability is within sight rather than hypothetical.
Custom manufacturing procurement is still mostly done by phone and email, so the addressable market for automated quoting is very large.
Eleven analysts average a $125.55 target, about 13% above the current price.
watch: Gross margin alongside revenue growth. Growing a marketplace is easy if you underprice; the test for Xometry is whether it can keep growing while the margin on each job widens.
